t: Concatenation of Array: Build nums + nums in One Pass
o:
**Understanding the problem**

Given nums of length n, we must return ans of length 2n where ans[i] = nums[i] and ans[i + n] = nums[i] — literally the array followed by a copy of itself. For nums = [1,2,1] the answer is [1,2,1,1,2,1]; for nums = [1,3,2,1] it is [1,3,2,1,1,3,2,1]. The constraints (n <= 1000) impose no performance pressure; the only real work is getting the indexing right and allocating the output up front. Every element is written exactly once at two symmetric positions, so a single loop over i fills both slots simultaneously.
k: ans[i] and ans[i + n] always receive the same value, so one pass over i in [0, n) writes two slots.
Language built-ins (list concatenation, Arrays.copyOf, vector::insert, spread syntax) express the whole operation in a single call.

a.n: Approach 1: Fill Two Slots Per Element
a.i: Allocate the result of size 2n, then iterate i from 0 to n-1 assigning nums[i] to both ans[i] and ans[i+n]. This makes the mirror-position structure explicit and avoids any reliance on library copy routines. It is the version interviewers usually want to see first.
s: For each i in [0, n): set ans[i] = nums[i] and ans[i + n] = nums[i].
a.t: O(n) — one pass writing two entries per iteration.
a.sp: O(n) — the output array of length 2n (output space is not counted as auxiliary by most conventions).

a.i: Every language ships a primitive that duplicates or joins sequences: Python list addition, JavaScript concat/spread, C++ vector insert, and Java copyOf plus arraycopy. Delegating to these yields minimal code and typically the fastest constant factors since they map to bulk memory copies.
s: Append another copy of nums using the language's native join/copy primitive.
a.t: O(n) — a single bulk copy of n elements.

w: Pick Approach 1 when asked to reason explicitly about indices, and Approach 2 for brevity in production code. Pitfalls: allocating n instead of 2n, off-by-one on ans[i + n], and mutating the input when reusing its storage. Likely follow-ups: concatenate k copies (still O(kn)), rotate by k positions before duplicating, or produce the result without extra allocation when in-place mutation is allowed.
